messages.author: 65b4deb3555c44c0
messages.subject: Proper analysis of butterfly data
parts:
Good evening everyone,

I am in the process of analyzing a dataset consisting of 192 butterfly counts (12 samples from 16 sites, 8 treatments + 8 controls, conducted in approximately 20 days), and I would appreciate your insights. 

I am trying to disentangle three processes that determined the observed number of butterflies at each transect count:
(i) detection probability,  butterflies are more active at certain environmental conditions 
(ii) date, butterflies abundance follows a unimodal trend during the species flight period
(iii) habitat type, control vs. treatment.

My original idea was to use the explicit hierarchical N-mixture model presented in Kery and Schaub 2012 (chapter 12), grouping the 12 samples in 6 groups of 2 days each, and modeling the abundance in each of the 6 "closed" periods. My samples were conducted in periods of 2 days, so this approach makes sense, but I probably counted some individuals in more than one of the 6 periods (butterflies likely survived longer than the period between "closed" counts). 

Is there any model that you would recommend to deal with this dataset, or any approach to relax broken assumptions tin the model that I am testing?

Thank you for your time and consideration, much appreciated.
Cheers,
Federico

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: Proper analysis of butterfly data
parts:
Dear Federico,

so what's exactly the temporal schedule of your surveys ? For one particular site, samples on days 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, ..... or what ?

If you have something like this, then I think that a binomial N-mixture model may be OK, i.e., you could treat the 'twin-days' as a period of closure, which enables you to estimate detection probability separately from abundance. In other words, you treat your design as a 'robust design' with 6 primary periods and 2 secondary periods per primary period.

You could then estimate detection probability for every secondary period (for a total of 12) and abundance for every primary period (for a total of 6). You could then estimate abundance separately for every primary period or put a quadratic trend on the N's to accommodate the expected unimodal trend in abundance.

You don't have a wonderful degree of replication along the spatial dimension: 16 sites is near the bottom end of what Nmix and occ models are typically applied, but it could be done. You could also complement your real-data analysis with some simulations to better understand how good the estimator from your desired model are likely to be with your particular sample sizes.

Best regards  --- Marc
